In this paper, we introduce Balanced-Reservoir Replay (BRR), a simple modification to reservoir sampling that preserves minority-class examples when the buffer is full. We evaluated BRR on the eICU-CRD dataset (2,520 patients, 8.37% mortality) using only age and gender, in a task-incremental setup with eight tasks and buffer sizes ranging from 0 to 1000 samples.Using a 1000-sample buffer (~\u200940% of past data), BRR outperformed standard sequential training, achieving an average AUC of 0.628\u2009\u00b1\u20090.019 compared to 0.610\u2009\u00b1\u20090.016 (p\u2009<\u20090.01). We conducted a sensitivity analysis of eight configurations of training duration (40 vs. 80 epochs per task) and forgetting penalties (\u03bb\u2009=\u20090.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0) supported the validity of this selection.This work questions the idea of minimal memory in continual learning. It indicates that retaining some past data can improve accuracy, enhance stability, and help meet regulatory requirements for slowly changing, low-data clinical tasks. for long-term time series forecasting are typically trained once and deployed as static predictors, despite operating in environments where data distributions continuously evolve. This mismatch between offline training and online deployment leads to progressive performance degradation and limits the practical adoption of modern forecasting models in real-world applications. To address this challenge, we formalize a continual learning (CL) for long-term time series forecasting problem, as a deployment-time adaptation problem and propose a model-agnostic framework enabling existing forecasting architectures to evolve without requiring storage of the entire historical dataset. Moreover we propose a new hybrid continual learning strategy that relies on a efficient use of knowledge distillation driven with a new attention-driven replay mechanism that continuously learns which historical sequences should be preserved for future adaptation, under memory constraints. Experiments conducted on state-of-the-art forecasting architectures, standard forecasting benchmarks, and real-world piezometric datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves forecasting accuracy while better preserving previously acquired knowledge than existing continual learning and adaptation strategies.
